papers.title: Sleep Duration Phenotypes and Dynamic Homeostasis: A Wave-Model Framework.
papers.abstract: Are sleep duration and sleep intensity manifestations of the same phenotype, or are they distinct, complementary traits? We addressed this question by removing two major constraints on phenotype expression: limited sleep opportunity and prior sleep deficit. Across 105 baseline 8-h nights and 420 extended 14-h nights in 15 individuals, sleep duration and NREM intensity behaved as two largely independent traits. Baseline expression of each parameter predicted its own subsequent expression during chronic sleep abundance but failed to predict the companion trait either within or between conditions. We then evaluated external evidence from chronic 4- and 6-h sleep restriction alongside extreme natural sleep-duration phenotypes, interpreting these findings through the wave model of sleep dynamics. In this framework, sleep duration reflects the geometry of sleep-cycle oscillations, determined primarily by the width of the sleep-state stability landscape (formally represented as a Morse potential well). Conversely, NREM intensity reflects oscillation amplitude, providing a visible signature of deviation from homeostatic equilibrium. While acute perturbation alters amplitude, chronic perturbation induces adaptive changes in landscape width, preserving a characteristic deviation from equilibrium despite severe shifts in underlying state instability and allostatic strain.

papers.title: Cross-Band Coupling of EEG Infraslow Oscillations during NREM Sleep in Mice.
papers.abstract: The infraslow oscillation (ISO) is a ~ 0.02 Hz rhythmic fluctuation in electroencephalographic (EEG) power during NREM sleep. Prior studies were limited to sigma-band ISO, linked to rhythmic norepinephrine release in mice. Whether ISOs exist in other bands, and how ISOs across bands are coupled, remain unknown. We analyzed cross-band ISO coupling across six frequency bands during NREM using a wild-type (WT) discovery dataset of 122 recordings from 72 mice and WT validation of 7 mice. A transgenic (TG) validation of 6 mice was added to test ISO coupling's robustness to Cre knock-in on the LepR gene (LepR-Cre). Band power time series were filtered to the ISO range of 0.01-0.03 Hz. Cross-band coupling was assessed using Spearman's correlation and phase-locking value (PLV) across all 15 band pairs. ISOs were strongest in alpha, sigma, beta, and theta bands, weak in gamma, and absent in delta. Alpha, sigma, beta, and theta ISOs formed a highly correlated motif with replication in WT and TG (r = 0.61-0.77), while gamma had moderate correlation (r = 0.30-0.42), and delta was uncorrelated (p > 0.05). All band pairs showed significant phase locking with replication (FDR-corrected q < 0.01), with stronger consistency in alpha, sigma, theta, and beta (PLV 0.54-0.71), and weaker consistency involving delta and gamma (PLV 0.12-0.37). EEG ISOs extend beyond the sigma band to alpha, beta, and theta bands, forming a strongly coupled motif that may reflect a fundamental organization principle of sleep microstructures at a minute scale.

papers.title: Behavioral evidence for two-stage sleep in spiders.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a fundamental behavioral state found across the animal kingdom, yet most of what we know about sleep is heavily vertebrate-biased. Studies are scarce or nonexistent in all but a few invertebrate lineages. A recent study of an REM sleep-like behavior in a jumping spider has reported unexpected parallels to sleep expression in vertebrates. So far, experimental evidence that these behavioral indicators truly represent sleep was lacking in spiders. Here, we present a comprehensive investigation into sleep behavior in the spider Portia fimbriata (Salticidae). We demonstrate diurnal activity, a free-running circadian rhythm, robust sleep architecture, regularly occurring REM-like behaviors, elevated arousal thresholds during those REM-like states, as well as rebound effects following sleep disruption. We conclude that the behavior we observe in spiders is behavioral sleep, providing evidence for an REM-like sleep substate in a terrestrial invertebrate. These results contribute to fundamental questions about the evolution and function of sleep across animals.

papers.title: High-fat diet-induced MAFLD is associated with sleep architecture disruption via hippocampal neuroinflammation and bifurcated IRS-1/Akt/mTOR signaling in mice.
papers.abstract: Epidemiological associations between metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) and sleep disturbances point to shared mechanisms, yet the underlying central pathways remain unexplored. We hypothesized that high-fat diet (HFD)-induced MAFLD disrupts sleep architecture via hippocampal neuroinflammation and dysregulation of the IRS-1/Akt/mTOR signaling axis. Male BALB/c mice were fed a control diet (CD) or a 60% HFD for 16 weeks to induce MAFLD. Sleep-wake architecture was assessed by 24-h EEG/EMG recordings. We evaluated hepatic steatosis, serum cytokines, hippocampal histology, and hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines. Hippocampal expression and phosphorylation of IRS-1 (Ser307), Akt (Ser473), and mTOR (Ser2448) were analyzed by Western blot. HFD-fed mice developed hepatic steatosis, elevated liver enzymes, and increased serum tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β). These mice exhibited reduced non‑rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep duration, severe sleep fragmentation (reflected by increased bout numbers and shorter mean bout durations), and diminished NREM sleep delta power. Cosinor analysis revealed a dampened circadian rhythm of NREM sleep delta power. In the hippocampus, HFD induced neuronal injury, elevated TNF-α and IL-1β levels, accompanied by a bifurcated signaling profile: increased p-IRS-1 (Ser307), decreased p-Akt (Ser473), and elevated p-mTOR (Ser2448). Our findings identify a putative liver-hippocampus-sleep axis in which MAFLD-driven systemic inflammation and hippocampal IRS-1/Akt/mTOR dysregulation are associated with profound sleep disruption, providing a framework for future mechanistic validation. Targeting this axis may offer new therapeutic strategies for sleep disorders in MAFLD.

papers.title: Automated Sleep Staging Performance Across Two Experimental Sleep Manipulation Protocols in Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging algorithms improve the scalability of polysomnography analysis in adolescent research but are primarily validated in undisturbed, single-night sleep recordings. It remains unclear whether these algorithms maintain performance when sleep architecture is experimentally manipulated. This study evaluated the validity of two popular automated sleep staging approaches across two distinct sleep manipulation paradigms in adolescents: a sleep restriction protocol (N=43, mean age [SD]=13.37[1.06] years; four nights including two sleep extension [10hr] and two restriction [4hr] nights) and a slow-wave sleep deprivation (SWSD) protocol (N=18, mean age [SD]=17.17[1.79] years; baseline, SWSD, and recovery nights). Automated sleep staging was performed using the POPulation-level Sleep Stager (POPS), the Yet Another Spindle Algorithm (YASA), and combined POPS+YASA. Manual polysomnography scoring by experienced sleep technicians served as the reference standard. Agreement was assessed using Cohen's k, and stage-specific performance was evaluated using F1 scores and confusion matrices. Mixed-effects models tested differences in overall and stage-specific agreement across nights. All staging approaches demonstrated moderate-to-substantial agreement with manual scoring across manipulated sleep conditions (k range; range=0.53-0.76). In the sleep restriction study, agreement was lower in restricted versus extended sleep (P<0.05), and agreement declined across restriction nights, with poorer Wake, N1, and N2 classification, while N3 remained preserved. In the SWSD study, overall agreement was lower on the SWSD night, with poorer N3 classification while other stages were preserved. Automated sleep staging performance may be less consistent in adolescents when sleep is curtailed or fragmented; future studies should develop and validate these algorithms under multiple sleep conditions.

papers.title: Auditory Evoked Potentials Across Cognitive States: Awake, Sleep, Sedation, and Anesthesia.
papers.abstract: Auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) comprise a family of electrophysiological responses that follow acoustic stimulation from the auditory nerve and brainstem to thalamocortical and association networks. Their interpretive value lies in the combination of millisecond temporal resolution and hierarchical sensitivity: early responses mainly index the fidelity and timing of ascending sensory conduction, whereas later responses increasingly depend on cortical context, attention, prediction, and behavioral relevance. This review develops a state-aware framework for interpreting AEPs during wakefulness, natural sleep, pharmacologic sedation, general anesthesia, and impaired consciousness. We first describe the ascending auditory pathway and relate approximate latency ranges to distributed neural generators. We then examine how attention and task engagement modify early cortical processing; how non-rapid eye movement and rapid eye movement sleep preserve some forms of acoustic analysis while reorganizing or suppressing others; and how anesthetic effects vary with response latency, drug concentration, and cortical hierarchy. The review also distinguishes transient event-related potentials from steady-state auditory evoked potentials (SSAEPs), and explains why phase-locked activity can be recovered by trial averaging whereas non-phase-locked induced activity requires single-trial time-frequency analysis. Separate sections address cross-species translation; click, chirp, oddball, steady-state, and naturalistic speech paradigms; as well as clinical applications in hearing assessment, intraoperative monitoring, anesthesia, and disorders of consciousness. The central conclusion is that an AEP is interpretable only when its generator, stimulus, analysis domain, recording conditions, and cognitive state are considered together.

papers.title: Characterising sleep spindle emergence in infancy: Effects of prematurity and early locomotor intervention
papers.abstract: Study objectives: Sleep spindles are thalamocortical oscillations evolving during early brain maturation. In adults, they support memory consolidation and are organised into rhythmic "trains" thought to support memory reactivation. How this temporal organisation emerges in infancy, and whether prematurity or early sensorimotor experience shapes it, remains unclear. This study characterised infant spindles and investigated how prematurity and early locomotor training affect their temporal and spatial organisation, providing insight into early brain maturation. Methods: Daytime high-density EEG sleep recordings were analysed in 50 infants born full-term (n=12) or very preterm (n=38, including 12 who received locomotor training) at 2 months corrected age. Spindle temporal organisation was analysed using a two-step Morlet wavelet transform to quantify slow modulations of spindle-band power (11-16Hz). Time-frequency decomposition around spindle onset was used to identify significant spindle-band scalp-wide activity, and topographical maps were statistically compared between groups. Results: All groups showed rhythmic spindle organisation, three times slower than in adults, with no group differences. Untrained preterm infants showed a more diffuse spindle-band activity than the distinct frontal and central clusters observed in full-term infants. Trained preterm infants exhibited a spatial distribution closely resembling that of full-term infants, although their frontal spindle density was lower than in both other groups. Conclusions: Spindle rhythmic organisation emerged early in infancy and remained unaffected by prematurity or locomotor training. Prematurity was associated with more diffuse spindle-band activity, suggesting reduced cortical specialisation, whereas trained preterm infants showed a spatial distribution resembling that of full-term infants, suggesting that early locomotor experience may influence thalamocortical organisation.

papers.title: Subchronic Sleep Fragmentation Induces Endocrine Alterations and Depression-like Behavior in Male Rats.
papers.abstract: Sleep fragmentation, a hallmark of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), has been linked to mood disorders through disrupted neuroendocrine regulation. However, the time-dependent development of depression-like behaviors and hormonal changes following recurrent sleep fragmentation remains unclear. This study examined the effects of repeated experimental sleep fragmentation on depression-like behavior and endocrine status in male Wistar rats. Twenty-four male Wistar rats were randomly assigned to three experimental groups (n = 8 per group): treadmill control (TC; stationary treadmill), activity control (AC; 10-min running/30-min resting cycles), and sleep fragmentation (SF; 30-s running/90-s resting cycles). Treatments were applied daily for 14 consecutive days during the first 6 h of the light phase. Depression-like behavior was assessed via the forced swimming test on days 1, 7, and 14. Body weight was monitored throughout, and serum corticosterone and testosterone were measured at the endpoint. Sleep architecture was inferred from the treadmill protocol rather than directly recorded. SF rats showed progressive increases in immobility and decreases in swimming and climbing over 14 days, reflecting the gradual emergence of depression-like behavior. SF animals also exhibited significantly reduced body-weight gain, elevated corticosterone (p < 0.01), and reduced testosterone (p < 0.001) compared with controls. Subchronic sleep fragmentation induced a progressive depression-like phenotype accompanied by neuroendocrine alterations, suggesting that recurrent sleep interruptions relevant to OSA may contribute to depression-associated endocrine dysregulation. Because sleep architecture was not directly recorded and hormones were measured only at the endpoint, these findings should be interpreted as associative rather than mechanistic.

papers.title: NREM sleep microarchitecture is associated with internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning in early adolescence.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common in youth with anxiety disorders, yet most prior work relies on subjective measures and does not capture underlying neural processes. We examined whether alterations in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep oscillations are present in children with anxiety disorders and whether these features relate to internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning. Children aged 9-13 years with diagnosed anxiety disorders (ANX; n = 17) and typically developing non-psychiatric comparison participants (NC; n = 26) completed overnight polysomnography. Slow oscillations (SO) and slow and fast sleep spindles were characterized using validated automated detection algorithms. Participants also completed a pre-sleep emotional processing task, and parents provided standardized measures of youth mental health. Group differences and dimensional associations between NREM oscillations, internalizing symptoms, and behavioral indices of emotional processing were examined. Sleep architecture did not differ between groups. Slow spindle duration was shorter in the ANX group. Across the full sample, shorter slow spindle duration was associated with greater internalizing symptoms, whereas higher SO density was positively associated with internalizing symptoms. Children in the ANX group exhibited greater facial emotional arousal and more frequent look-away behavior during the emotional processing task. Across participants, greater emotional arousal and look-away behavior were associated with shorter spindle duration during subsequent sleep. Specific features of NREM microarchitecture were associated with individual differences in internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning during early adolescence. These findings highlight the potential relevance of NREM oscillations for understanding developmental links between sleep and youth psychopathology. Sleep disturbances are common in youth with anxiety disorders, yet most research has relied on subjective reports and broad measures of sleep quality. This study demonstrates that specific features of non-rapid eye movement sleep microarchitecture, particularly sleep spindle duration, are associated with anxiety, depression, and emotional responding during early adolescence even in the absence of differences in overall sleep quality or sleep stage distribution. These findings highlight the importance of examining neural features of sleep when investigating emotional functioning and internalizing psychopathology during development. More broadly, the results suggest that adolescence may represent a sensitive developmental window during which alterations in sleep physiology are linked to emotional functioning. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine how these sleep features relate to developmental trajectories of youth psychopathology.

papers.title: REM sleep infraslow rhythms correlate with neuropsychiatric symptom severity.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is commonly divided into phasic and tonic substates based on higher and lower oculomotor activity, respectively. Our previous study described an alternative framework in which REM temporal structure forms a continuum of infraslow rhythms (∼0.01 Hz) across brain and body physiology. We now ask whether these infraslow rhythms vary with neuropsychiatric symptoms, given the long-standing but still inconsistent links between REM and mood- or trauma-related disorders. Using a cross-sectional polysomnographic dataset from male veterans, we examined 59 participants for correlations between REM infraslow rhythms and neuropsychiatric symptom scores, excluding participants with moderate/severe apnea. Oscillations in REM respiratory rate, but not cardiac rate or electroencephalogram beta power, showed higher infraslow frequencies in participants with multiple symptoms, including posttraumatic stress, pain, anxiety, depression, and cognitive difficulties. No significant correlations were found between these symptoms and conventional REM metrics (e.g., REM density, latency and duration). To further examine REM beyond phasic/tonic binarization, we analyzed the timing between oculomotor activity and infraslow oscillations. Eye movements occurred preferentially during periods of high respiratory rate, low beta power and intermediate cardiac rate, with no changes in these temporal relationships across symptom severity. Neuropsychiatric associations with REM infraslow rhythms spanned multiple symptom domains but were physiologically specific, with respiratory rate oscillations representing the strongest readout of symptom burden. Furthermore, REM infraslow cycles across brain and body were differentially aligned with eye movements: a temporal pattern that may serve as a physiological target for neuropsychiatric and mechanistic research. Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep has long been studied in relation to neuropsychiatric conditions, but traditional measures of the timing and duration of REM episodes have shown limited consistency for symptom tracking. This study addresses this gap by highlighting a less explored physiological feature within REM episodes: minute-scale, or infraslow, rhythms in respiratory and cardiac rate, as well as oculomotor and brain activity. We report that REM infraslow oscillations, particularly in respiratory rate, occur at higher frequency in participants with worse trauma/mood symptoms and cognitive difficulties. This work is evidence of a possible new REM sleep-based biomarker for multiple diseases.

papers.title: Mechanisms of auditory cortex injury and the protective effects of reoxygenation in a rat model of intermittent hypoxia.
papers.abstract: Intermittent hypoxia associated with obstructive sleep apnea can impair auditory function, but the early mechanisms underlying auditory cortical injury and the extent to which these changes recover after the restoration of normoxia remain unclear. This study investigated the mechanisms underlying auditory cortical injury in a rat model of intermittent hypoxia and evaluated the protective effects of reoxygenation. Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats were assigned to control, intermittent hypoxia, intermittent hypoxia followed by 1 week of normoxic recovery, or control followed by normoxic recovery groups. Short-term intermittent hypoxia caused high-frequency hearing loss and increased spontaneous firing in the primary auditory cortex. After 1 week of normoxic recovery, auditory thresholds and cortical firing rates returned to levels comparable to those in the control group. Glutamate levels did not differ significantly among the groups, whereas γ-aminobutyric acid and 5-hydroxytryptamine levels were elevated in the intermittent hypoxia followed by normoxic recovery group. Intermittent hypoxia increased superoxide dismutase activity, reduced catalase activity, and elevated the levels of tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and interleukin-6. Normoxic recovery normalized catalase activity and reduced tumor necrosis factor-α and interleukin-6 levels, whereas superoxide dismutase activity and interleukin- 1β levels remained elevated. Metabolomic analysis identified alterations in unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis, branched-chain amino acid metabolism, ferroptosis-related pathways, redox-related metabolism, and amino acid and protein turnover, several of which persisted after recovery. These findings indicate that acute intermittent hypoxia-induced auditory dysfunction and cortical hyperexcitability are reversible, whereas redox, inflammatory, and metabolic abnormalities recover asynchronously. Persistent molecular disturbances after functional recovery may provide potential targets for further investigation of obstructive sleep apnea-associated central auditory injury.

papers.title: Early Time-Restricted Eating, Circadian Alignment, and Cognitive Preservation in Older Adults: A Neurobiological Hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Nearly half of dementia cases are attributed to fourteen modifiable risk factors listed by the 2024 Lancet Commission; meal timing is not among them. Disrupted daily (circadian) rhythms are linked to faster neurodegeneration, yet it is unknown whether meal timing affects cognitive ageing. We review the evidence for the hypothesis that early time-restricted eating (eTRE) helps preserve cognition in older adults. We define eTRE as eating within a window of no more than 10 h, with at least 80% of daily energy eaten before 16:00. We evaluate three candidate pathways: daily rhythms in the removal of amyloid-beta and tau from the brain (glymphatic clearance), daily rhythms that keep brain inflammation low, and clock genes that support memory-related plasticity in the hippocampus. Nutrient-sensing and gut microbiota pathways are considered as alternatives. An AI co-scientist analysis, checked by the authors, suggested a "Dual-Gating" model: finishing meals early may lower nervous-system arousal and insulin levels at night, and both changes may favour brain clearance during sleep. We outline a three-arm trial (eTRE, late time-restricted eating, habitual eating) that tests whether any cognitive benefit is explained by changes in markers of clearance and inflammation. Meal timing remains a candidate exposure that needs prospective testing.

papers.title: Compensatory drive and sleep-related phantom limb pain: the moderating role of autonomic reserve.
papers.abstract: Phantom limb pain (PLP) is common after amputation, yet why poor sleep becomes pain in only some individuals is unknown. We hypothesized that a regulatory response is interpretable only against the reserve sustaining it, and thus we tested whether autonomic capacity relative to demand moderates the sleep-pain relationship in 121 amputee adults. Sleep was assessed with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index; PLP, residual limb pain (RLP), and phantom limb sensation (PLS) on 0-10 scales. Heart rate variability was summarized as autonomic reserve (log-transformed SDNN, RMSSD, total and high-frequency power) and autonomic drive (normalized low-frequency power). Poorer sleep was associated with greater PLP and RLP, but not PLS. No single HRV index moderated these associations, but the sleep × reserve × drive interaction did for PLP (b = -0.51, p = 0.026). Poor sleep predicted pain most strongly under high drive with reduced reserve. PLP vulnerability reflects autonomic capacity relative to demand, instead of any single HRV marker alone.

papers.title: Skin-Interfaced Flexible Sensors for Continuous Monitoring of Thermal, Mechanical, Electrical, and Respiratory Signals.
papers.abstract: Skin-interfaced flexible sensors enable physiological monitoring during daily activities, sleep, and rehabilitation, but a sensitive device or a clear waveform does not by itself establish the validity of the physiological information obtained. Many existing reviews emphasize sensor materials, fabrication, device design, and sensing performance. This review instead examines how physiological information is preserved or altered from its origin to its eventual interpretation. We focus on flexible physical sensors for skin temperature, mechanical activity, surface biopotentials, electrodermal activity, and respiration-related monitoring. The scope is restricted to selected physical and skin surface electrical sensing pathways, while optical, biochemical, and implantable technologies are not reviewed in detail. The analysis links the physical quantity available at the skin to its transmission across the skin-device interface, sensor response, signal fidelity, and the physiological output that the measurement can reasonably support. This approach distinguishes direct measurements from derived or clinically interpreted quantities and shows where additional reference-based validation becomes necessary. Across the reviewed modalities, major limitations arise when interface conditions or environmental and mechanical interference alter the relationship between the physiological source and the recorded signal. Reliable monitoring therefore depends on preserving this relationship under intended wearing conditions and demonstrating agreement with references appropriate to the claimed output. By focusing on this measurement process, the review complements materials- and device-oriented surveys and provides a basis for judging flexible sensors according to the physiological information that their measurements can support.

papers.title: The Raine Study: a multigenerational Western Australian birth and life-course cohort advancing research on the developmental origins of health and disease.
papers.abstract: The Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) framework has transformed understanding of how early-life exposures shape health across the life course, yet populations from Oceania remain underrepresented in this research. The Raine Study is a globally unique, multigenerational longitudinal pregnancy cohort established in Western Australia, one of the world's most geographically isolated regions. The study recruited 2900 pregnant women (Generation1) in 1989, which resulted in 2868 live births forming Generation 2, and is now currently recruiting Generation 3 (the children of Generation 2). This paper describes the evolution of the Raine Study from its origins as a pregnancy cohort grounded in DOHaD to a comprehensive life-course and multigenerational research resource. This resource has led to key research findings that have informed international clinical guidelines and national and state health policies across areas including prenatal development and care safety, neurodevelopment, cardiometabolic health, obesity, liver disease, physical activity, mental health, sedentary behaviour, sleep, and assisted reproductive technologies. Central to the Raine Study's success is a longstanding commitment to participant partnership and engagement, resulting in exceptional retention and strong consumer involvement in governance and research prioritisation. The Raine Study demonstrates the critical value of well-characterised, place-based cohorts for advancing DOHaD and life-course science and provides a globally significant resource to inform prevention strategies, precision medicine, and public health policy across generations.

papers.title: The Influence of Sleep and Autonomic Recovery on Performance in World-Class Swimmers at Major Competitions: The Qualifying Trials, World Championships, and Olympic Games.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation is one of the main risk factors for impaired performance in elite athletes, but the changes in sleep and autonomic regulation in response to competitions of varying levels within the same Olympic year remain unknown. In this prospective, longitudinal, observational study, we monitored parameters related to sleep quality and quantity, as well as heart rate variability and resting heart rate, in a cohort of eight Olympic swimmers (n = 8) during the World Championships in Doha, the qualifying trials, and the 2024 Paris Olympic Games, using the Oura Ring Gen3 under real-world conditions throughout the pre-competition, competition, and post-competition phases of each event. The Olympic Games were the only event where sleep efficiency fell below the commonly used reference threshold of 85% during the competition phase accompanied by a reduction in the total sleep score and an increase in resting heart rate. The Olympic setting was accompanied by temporary changes in sleep and autonomic markers, but no sleep parameter or autonomic marker showed a statistically significant association with intra-individual competitive performance, although the limited sample size constrains the power to detect such relationships.

papers.title: A Complementary Dual-Branch Receptive Field Network for Cross-Channel-Density Motor Imagery EEG Decoding.
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable direct communication between the brain and external devices, providing a bio-inspired link between humans and artificial systems. However, electroencephalography (EEG)-based motor imagery (MI) decoding continues to pose challenges, due to limited temporal exploitation and insufficient spatio-temporal modeling. To alleviate these limitations, a complementary dual-branch receptive field network (DBRFNet) is proposed for cross-channel-density MI-EEG decoding. Specifically, two complementary branches with distinct temporal receptive fields are designed to capture multi-scale temporal dynamics. Each branch employs a progressive spatio-temporal module integrating temporal, depthwise spatial, and dilated convolutions for modeling short- and long-range temporal dependencies. The features from the two branches are fused using element-wise addition and further encoded for classification. The proposed method is evaluated on three public datasets representing low-, medium-, and high-density EEG configurations. DBRFNet achieves decoding accuracies of 80.48%, 84.37%, and 92.24% under cross-validation analysis, and 87.76%, 80.94%, and 94.64% under hold-out analysis, demonstrating competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each component within the proposed architecture. These results indicate that DBRFNet effectively learns discriminative spatio-temporal representations and provides a robust solution for MI-BCI systems.

papers.title: Integrated assessment of driving performance, eye movements, and cognitive function in obstructive sleep apnea: A pilot study.
papers.abstract: Motor vehicle accident (MVA) risk is greater in patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), yet the functional domains most closely linked to driving-related impairment remain incompletely understood. This exploratory pilot study aimed to perform an integrated assessment of driving performance, eye movements, vigilance, and cognitive function in OSA and to examine their relationships with disease severity and treatment response. Adult drivers with suspected OSA underwent assessment using a driving simulator, Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT), eye-tracking, and the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB). Participants with moderate-to-severe OSA (apnea-hypopnea index ≥20) who initiated continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy underwent re-evaluation after 6-12 months. At baseline, single-task reaction time in the driving simulator was positively correlated with apnea severity. In contrast, response accuracy under multitask plus steering conditions was associated with nocturnal hypoxemia (T90), suggesting differential contributions of apnea frequency and oxygen desaturation to driving performance. Eye-tracking parameters, including saccade amplitude and fixation duration, were significantly correlated with both driving performance and spatial working memory error scores. Following CPAP therapy, simple reaction times improved in both the driving simulator and PVT, whereas changes in multitasking performance and CANTAB measures were not statistically significant. Basic psychomotor speed was associated with OSA severity and improved following CPAP therapy, suggesting within-subject improvement of vigilance-dependent processes. In contrast, integrated oculomotor and executive function measures were more closely linked to complex driving performance, indicating that multidomain assessment may better characterize driving-related impairment in OSA. These findings provide preliminary evidence to guide future hypothesis-driven studies.

papers.title: Effects of Maternal Caffeine Exposure During Gestation on Neurobehavior, Glucose Metabolism and Circadian Rhythm in Offspring Rats.
papers.abstract: Caffeine intake can have numerous effects on neurological and cognitive impairments. However, its influences on offspring still need to be evaluated. This study aimed to investigate the effects of caffeine exposure during gestation on behavioral development, metabolic function, and circadian rhythms in offspring. A total of 96 Sprague-Dawley rats were included, with an equal number of males and females. After confirming pregnancy, the female rats were randomly divided into four groups on average and administered caffeine at three distinct doses (5, 20, and 80 mg/kg/day) or equivalent volumes of normal saline throughout the gestational period. The health status and weight gain of pregnant rats, as well as the litter size and body weight of offspring, were continuously monitored. Open field test, Morris water maze, intraperitoneal glucose tolerance tests (IPGTT) and intraperitoneal insulin tolerance tests (IPITTs) were performed. The expression levels of 7 circadian clock genes (Bmal1, Clock, Cry1, Cry2, Per1, Per2, and Rev-erbα) were quantified. This revealed a significant reduction in maternal weight gain in the 80 mg/kg caffeine group compared to controls. Although the birth weight of offspring was not significantly affected, the postnatal weight gain of offspring was slower in caffeine groups. Behavioral assessments demonstrated elevated spontaneous activity and increased anxiety-like behaviors in caffeine-exposed offspring. Metabolic evaluations indicated impaired glucose tolerance specifically in female offspring, though no significant alterations were observed in insulin sensitivity, spatial learning and memory performance. Maternal caffeine exposure during gestation also disrupted the rhythmicity of hepatic circadian clock gene expression in offspring rats. These findings suggest that gestational caffeine exposure exerts selective adverse effects on offspring development, behavior, glucose metabolism and circadian rhythm. Caffeine consumption during pregnancy necessitates careful consideration.

papers.title: Circadian-Based Optimization of Pharmacotherapy in Chronic Diseases: Integrating Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics, and Disease Rhythm.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are endogenous, approximately 24-hour biological cycles that regulate physiological processes, including cardiovascular function, metabolism, immune activity, endocrine signaling, and sleep-wake patterns. These rhythms significantly influence disease pathophysiology and therapeutic responses, making biological time an important determinant of treatment outcomes. Several chronic diseases, including cardiovascular disorders, asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, metabolic syndrome, and psychiatric conditions, exhibit predictable circadian variations in symptom severity and disease activity. Simultaneously, circadian oscillations affect pharmacokinetic processes such as drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, as well as pharmacodynamic mechanisms involving receptor sensitivity and cellular responsiveness. As a result, identical drug doses administered at different times may produce considerable differences in efficacy and toxicity. This review analyzes the role of circadian biology in optimizing pharmacotherapy through the integration of chronopharmacology and chronotherapy. It discusses the molecular basis of circadian regulation and its influence on physiological systems, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics. Disease-specific chronotherapeutic applications in cardiovascular, metabolic, endocrine, respiratory, rheumatologic, psychiatric, and oncologic disorders are highlighted. Clinical examples, including evening statin administration, timed bronchodilator use, and modified-release glucocorticoid therapy, highlight the practical benefits of circadian-based therapies. However, evidence remains variable across therapeutic areas, with some chronotherapeutic strategies, such as bedtime antihypertensive dosing, showing conflicting results in recent clinical trials. Further research is needed to define optimal timing recommendations and facilitate wider clinical adoption. Throughout, the strength of evidence is appraised to distinguish chronotherapeutic strategies with sufficient support for routine clinical use from those that remain experimental. The review also discusses emerging developments in chronopharmacokinetic modeling, advanced drug delivery systems, wearable monitoring devices, and precision chronomedicine. Despite promising evidence, broader implementation remains limited by variability in circadian patterns, lack of awareness, and insufficient standardized guidelines. Integrating circadian principles into pharmacotherapy and, ultimately, combining precision chronotherapy with lifestyle-based strategies may offer a promising direction for improving therapeutic precision, disease prevention, and patient outcomes.

papers.title: Assessment of Sleep Quality and Modifiable Disruptors in Postoperative Paediatric Patients: A Clinical Audit.
papers.abstract: Background Sleep disruption is common during postoperative hospitalisation and may be influenced by pain, overnight clinical care, and environmental factors. This quality improvement project assessed sleep quality among postoperative paediatric inpatients and identified potentially modifiable contributors to sleep disturbance. Methodology A clinical audit was conducted on a paediatric inpatient ward between April and June 2026. Children aged 0-18 years admitted following elective or emergency orthopaedic surgery and requiring at least one overnight postoperative stay were eligible. Parents or carers completed a questionnaire after the child's first postoperative night assessing sleep quality, nighttime awakenings, causes of sleep disturbance, ward noise and lighting, clustering of overnight care, assessment of sleep needs, and parent/carer sleep. Responses were analysed descriptively using frequencies and percentages. Results In total, 19 questionnaires were included: 14 from children accommodated in multi-bed bays and five from children in individual cubicles. In bays, eight of 14 (57.1%) children were reported to have fair sleep and six (42.9%) woke more than five times overnight. In cubicles, two of five (40.0%) children were reported to have good sleep and one (20.0%) woke more than five times. Nursing observations were reported as a contributor to sleep disturbance in 10 of 14 (71.4%) children in bays and four of five (80.0%) in cubicles. Pain contributed to sleep disturbance in 10 of 19 (52.6%) children overall. Most respondents reported that the ward was quiet overnight and that lights were kept low. However, only seven of 19 (36.8%) families reported being asked about their child's sleep needs. Parent/carer sleep was also frequently disrupted. Conclusions Postoperative sleep disruption was common, with nursing observations and pain among the most frequently reported contributors. Despite generally favourable perceptions of overnight noise and lighting, opportunities for improvement were identified in assessment of individual sleep needs, coordination of overnight care where clinically appropriate, and optimisation of pain management. A subsequent audit cycle following implementation of these measures will assess their impact on sleep-related outcomes.

papers.title: Circadian and Sex-Specific Responses to Alternaria alternata in Allergic Airway Inflammation.
papers.abstract: Asthma severity and immune responses are regulated by circadian rhythms, yet the role of circadian timing in fungal allergen-induced airway inflammation remains poorly defined. Alternaria alternata , a clinically relevant fungal allergen, is strongly associated with severe asthma exacerbations and persistent airway dysfunction. Using a preclinical mouse model, we investigated whether pulmonary responses to Alternaria exposure are influenced by time of day and sex. We demonstrate that Alternaria induces allergic airway inflammation, airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR), and epithelial barrier disruption in a circadian- and sex-dependent manner. Female mice exhibited enhanced eosinophilic, neutrophilic, interstitial macrophage, and dendritic cell infiltration predominantly at Zeitgeber Time 0 (ZT0), whereas males showed stronger inflammatory responses at ZT12. Alternaria exposure increased IL-33 release and promoted ILC2 and Th2 cell accumulation, with distinct temporal patterns between sexes. Cytokine and chemokine profiling revealed robust Th2, proinflammatory, and Th17 responses that varied with exposure time, with higher responses at ZT12 in females and ZT0 in males. Markers of tissue injury, including lactate dehydrogenase and uric acid, followed similar circadian-dependent trends. Functionally, Alternaria -exposed mice displayed greater AHR during the resting phase, particularly in males. Additionally, Alternaria disrupted epithelial junctional proteins (E-cadherin and ZO-1) and altered expression of core circadian clock proteins CLOCK, BMAL1, and REV-ERBα. Mechanistically, peak inflammation coincided with enhanced STAT1, STAT3, and STAT6 activation. Collectively, these findings identify circadian timing and sex as key determinants of fungal allergen-induced airway inflammation and suggest chronotherapeutic approaches may improve asthma outcomes.

papers.title: Maternal sleep deprivation is associated with fetal hypothalamic-hepatic remodeling and long-term metabolic and behavioral alterations in offspring.
papers.abstract: Maternal sleep deprivation (MSD) is increasingly prevalent during pregnancy; however, its long-term developmental impact on offspring health remains incompletely defined. Here, we identify MSD as a prenatal stressor that is associated with coordinated alterations in fetal hypothalamic-hepatic neuro-metabolic pathways, potentially contributing to increased vulnerability to metabolic and affective disorders later in life. Using a mouse model of chronic gestational sleep deprivation, we perform longitudinal metabolic and behavioral phenotyping in offspring combined with transcriptomic profiling of the fetal hypothalamus and liver and integrative analyses extending into adulthood. Female MSD offspring exhibit delayed-onset glucose intolerance, insulin resistance, and altered lipid utilization during aging, whereas male offspring display only mild metabolic alterations. MSD offspring also demonstrate alterations in anxiety-like and helplessness-related behavioral indices, which are further exacerbated by chronic stress exposure. Transcriptomic analyses reveal coordinated remodeling of hypothalamic neurodevelopmental and neurotransmitter pathways alongside hepatic metabolic programs during fetal development, suggesting early alterations of hypothalamic-liver coupling. Comparative analyses between fetal and adult liver samples demonstrate persistent dysregulation of metabolic pathways. Collectively, these findings suggest that MSD is associated with reconfiguration of fetal central-peripheral regulatory networks, which may contribute to a maladaptive neuro-metabolic trajectory linking metabolic and emotional dysfunction across the lifespan. These results identify prenatal sleep as a modifiable determinant of offspring health and provide insight into potential mechanisms underlying the shared developmental origins of metabolic and affective disorders.

papers.title: Cerebellar Continuous Theta Burst Stimulation for Insomnia Disorder: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the effects of cerebellar continuous theta burst stimulation (cTBS) in insomnia disorder (ID). In this randomized sham-controlled trial, patients with ID received 2 weeks of active or sham cerebellar cTBS. The primary outcome was a ≥ 3-point improvement in Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score after treatment. Secondary outcomes included changes in sleep, mood, and resting-state fMRI. Seventy-two patients (51 women; mean age, 44.3 ± 11.6 years) were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. More patients in the active than sham group achieved a ≥ 3-point PSQI improvement after treatment (75.0% vs. 33.3%; adjusted OR, 6.06; 95% CI, 2.17-18.50; p < 0.001). Active cTBS reduced PSQI scores versus sham both post-treatment (adjusted mean difference, -3.34; 95% CI, -4.57 to -2.12; p < 0.001) and at 1 month (-3.70; 95% CI, -4.93 to -2.48; p < 0.001), and also improved Insomnia Severity Index, Hamilton Anxiety Scale, and Hamilton Depression Scale at both time points (all p < 0.01). Exploratory fMRI analyses identified several post-treatment connectivity differences between groups, but only right amygdala-right orbitofrontal connectivity showed a significant group-by-time interaction (FDR-adjusted p = 0.038). No serious adverse events occurred. Cerebellar cTBS was well tolerated and promising for ID. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05992285).

papers.title: Bipolar Disorder and Epilepsy: Clinical and Neurobiological Overlaps, Evidence Gaps, and an Exploratory Systems Perspective.
papers.abstract: Accumulating evidence suggests that bipolar disorder (BD) and epilepsy share important clinical, neurobiological, and therapeutic features. Both disorders are characterized by recurrent episodes and fluctuating clinical courses, raising the possibility that partially overlapping or analogous regulatory processes may contribute to some aspects of their clinical expression and progression. This review examines current evidence regarding the overlap between BD and epilepsy and explores integrative perspectives that may help explain their similarities. A narrative review of the literature was conducted. Evidence related to genetics, neuroimaging, cognition, neuroplasticity, neuroinflammation, stress biology, network neuroscience, and treatment response was examined. Findings across BD and epilepsy reveal partially overlapping biological and clinical features, including alterations in excitation-inhibition balance, neuromodulatory disturbances, neuroinflammatory processes, and neuroplastic changes. Neuroimaging studies in both conditions reveal abnormalities in large-scale brain networks involved in emotional regulation, cognitive control, and behavioral adaptation. Clinically, both disorders show sensitivity to environmental and physiological stressors and sleep disruption, cognitive impairment, and partial responsiveness to overlapping pharmacological and neuromodulatory interventions. These observations are compatible with the hypothesis that recurrent episodes and prolonged network dysregulation may reinforce maladaptive patterns of instability through interacting feedback processes, although this interpretation remains to be tested directly. Current evidence identifies several clinical and biological similarities between BD and epilepsy but does not yet establish that these similarities reflect identical or directly shared causal mechanisms. An integrative perspective combining network dysfunction, neuroplasticity, and systemic regulatory processes may provide a useful heuristic framework for investigating disease heterogeneity, progression, and treatment response. Further longitudinal and comparative studies are required before this perspective can support personalized monitoring strategies or mechanism-informed interventions.

papers.title: Coping-Strategies as a Mediator Between Symptoms of Sleeping Problems and Risk of Suicide.
papers.abstract: Suicide is a complex, global phenomenon linked to various intersecting vulnerability factors. Among these, sleep-related symptoms represent a significant yet understudied contributor to suicide risk. This study explored whether the concurrent relationship between sleep-related symptoms and suicide risk is statistically mediated by distinct coping strategies within an exploratory cross-sectional framework, addressing data non-normality through robust analytical methods. A total of 1014 participants (33.83% male, 66.17% female) aged 18 to 75 years (M = 33.00, SD = 15.15) participated in an online survey distributed through snowball recruitment. Participants completed the amplified Sleep Symptom Subscale (Su-a) of the Brief Symptom Checklist (LSB-50), the Coping with Stress Questionnaire (CSQ), and the Risk of Suicide Scale (RS). Multiple mediation analyses were conducted to evaluate the indirect effects of coping dimensions while adjusting for sex, age, educational attainment, and socioeconomic status. Sleep-related symptoms were positively associated with suicide risk. Negative self-focus emerged as the strongest mediator (β = 0.112, 95% CI [0.083, 0.143]), whereas Positive Reappraisal (β = 0.018, 95% CI [0.007, 0.032]) and Seeking Social Support (β = 0.012, 95% CI [0.001, 0.024]) acted as protective mediators. Overt emotional expression also showed a small but significant indirect effect (β = 0.009, 95% CI [0.001, 0.018]). A significant direct effect of sleep-related symptoms on suicide risk remained, indicating partial mediation. The findings suggest that coping processes contribute to the connection between sleep difficulties and suicide risk. Interventions aimed at reducing maladaptive coping and strengthening adaptive coping skills may help diminish suicidal vulnerability among individuals experiencing sleep disturbances.

papers.title: Bridging the gap: advanced chromatin biotechnologies for circadian epigenomic profiling in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
papers.abstract: Surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy remain the main therapies for treating head and neck cancers, however new modalities have emerged with an emphasis to understand the complexity of the tumor biology. One emerging layer of complexity is the circadian clock, disrupted in many cancers, contributes to pathogenesis and progression due to its crosstalk with cancer pathways. While transcriptional alterations of core clock genes have been described in Head and Neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), the higher-order epigenetic and chromatin-based mechanisms underlying circadian dysregulation remain poorly defined. In this review, we highlight the potential of several chromatin-based biotechnologies in characterizing circadian clock disruption and identifying epigenetic biomarkers in HNSCC. Powerful assays including Chromatin conformation capture, Chromatin immunoprecipitation, DNA methylation profiling, ATAC-seq and single cell technologies can dissect circadian disruption at multiple regulatory layers. These approaches enable genome-wide mapping of chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and 3D chromatin organization. Integrating these approaches across HPV-positive (HPV+) and HPV-negative (HPV-) HNSCC provides a framework to determine whether circadian disruption reflects transcriptional deregulation alone or involved structural genome remodeling that actively drives tumor progression. Linking circadian disruption to epigenomic reprogramming in HNSCCs can serve to identify mechanisms of therapeutic resistance and identify vulnerabilities. Advancing chromatin-informed circadian biomarker discovery in HNSCC has the potential to shift precision oncology from static genomic profiling toward dynamic, architecture-based epigenetic regulation.

papers.title: Sleep Disturbances and Health-Related Quality of Life in Paediatric Oncology: A Comparative Study with Non-Oncological Chronic Illness and Healthy Peers.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Sleep disturbance is increasingly recognized as a key contributor to symptom burden and functioning in paediatric oncology, yet comparative evidence across clinical and healthy populations remains limited. This study examined sleep quality and its association with health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in children and adolescents with cancer compared with peers with non-oncological chronic illnesses and healthy controls. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted at Hong Kong Children's Hospital. Participants 6-18 years were recruited by convenience sampling into three groups (oncology, chronic illness, healthy; n = 50 each). Children and adolescents completed the Chinese Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Pediatrics Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) 4.0. Group differences were tested using chi-square tests and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with post hoc Tukey comparisons. Pearson correlations and hierarchical multiple linear regression examined PSQI-PedsQL associations. Results: Sleep quality differed significantly across groups (p < 0.001), with the poorest sleep observed in the oncology group. The prevalence of poor sleep (PSQI ≥ 5) was 60.0% in oncology group, compared with 40.0% in those with chronic illness and 30.0% in healthy peers. Mean global PSQI scores were 6.02 ± 3.40 in the oncology group, 4.10 ± 2.60 in the chronic illness group, and 3.30 ± 2.35 in healthy controls, with a significant overall group difference (p < 0.001). Impairments were most pronounced in sleep latency, habitual sleep efficiency, and sleep disturbances. HRQoL was lowest in the oncology group (p < 0.001). Mean PedsQL total scores were 68.98 ± 15.73 in the oncology group, 75.99 ± 14.03 in the chronic illness group, and 85.44 ± 10.26 in healthy controls, respectively, with a significant overall group difference (p < 0.001). Across the full sample, poor sleep quality was independently associated with lower HRQoL after adjustment for demographic and clinical factors (β = -0.271, p = 0.002), with no significant interaction by group. Conclusions: Children and adolescents with cancer reported clinically significant sleep impairment, driven mainly by reduced sleep quality and continuity. Routine sleep screening and targeted supportive interventions may improve HRQoL in paediatric oncology.

papers.title: Effects of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Combined With Perioperative Refined Nursing on Postoperative Sleep Disturbances, Anxiety, and Depression in Patients Undergoing Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting.
papers.abstract: To assess whether integrating mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) into refined perioperative nursing is associated with improvements in postoperative sleep disturbances, anxiety, and depression in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). We retrospectively reviewed 146 CABG patients treated at Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, from July 2023 to August 2025. To reduce selection bias, 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) was performed based on baseline characteristics, yielding 73 matched pairs for analysis. Based on the nursing protocol documented in the medical records, patients were classified into two groups: a standard care group had received standard refined perioperative nursing, while an MBSR group had received the same care supplemented with MBSR. Outcome measures included Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) scores assessed preoperatively and on postoperative day 7, objective sleep architecture indices obtained via actigraphy on the day of surgery and on postoperative day 7, length of hospital stay, time to first postoperative ambulation, incidence of sleep disturbances on postoperative day 7, and serum levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6), cortisol, orexin, and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) measured preoperatively and at 24 and 72 hours postoperatively. Statistical analyses included t-tests, repeated measures analysis of variance, and chi‑square tests. After PSM, 73 patients were included in each group, with all standardized mean differences <0.1. Baseline preoperative HADS scores did not differ between groups (p > 0.05). On postoperative day 7, bothgroups showed reductions in (HADS-Anxiety) HADS-A and HADS-Depression (HADS-D), with the MBSR group exhibiting significantly lower scores on all HADS subscales than the standard care group (p < 0.05). PSQI scores on the day of surgery were similar (p > 0.05); On postoperative day 7, both groups improved in total PSQI and across its seven domains versus the surgical day. The MBSR group had significantly better scores than the standard care group for all PSQI domains and total score except subjective sleep quality and hypnotic use(p < 0.05). Time to first postoperative ambulation was shorter and the rate of sleep disturbance on postoperative day 7 was lower in the MBSR group (p < 0.05); mean hospital stay did not differ (p > 0.05). Objective sleep parameters on the day of surgery were comparable (p > 0.05); on postoperative day 7 both groups showed increased total sleep time and sleep efficiency, with greater gains in the MBSR group (p < 0.05). Nighttime awakenings decreased in both groups, with the MBSR group showing a larger reduction (p < 0.05). Repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) revealed significant effects of time, group, and time-by-group interaction for cortisol, orexin, IL-6, and TNF-α (p < 0.05). Within-group analyses showed postoperative increases in cortisol, IL-6, and TNF-α at 24 and 72 hours and declines in orexin versus baseline (p < 0.05). Between-group comparisons at 24 and 72 hours postoperatively demonstrated lower cortisol, IL-6, and TNF-α and higher orexin in the MBSR group compared with the standard care group (p < 0.05), and the temporal patterns differed significantly between groups (p < 0.05). Refined perioperative nursing incorporating MBSR was associated with alleviation of negative emotions in patients undergoing CABG, a lower incidence of sleep disturbances on the 7th postoperative day, and shorter time to first postoperative ambulation.

papers.title: Cardiometabolic Substrate Modification in Atrial Fibrillation: Obesity and Epicardial Adipose Tissue in the Era of Incretin-Based Therapies and Catheter Ablation.
papers.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is increasingly understood as the electrical expression of a systemic and atrial cardiometabolic disease rather than an isolated disorder of pulmonary-vein triggers. Obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension, sleep-disordered breathing, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and visceral adiposity promote atrial stretch, inflammation, fibrosis, autonomic imbalance, and conduction heterogeneity. Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT), particularly the peri-left-atrial depot, may provide a local mechanistic bridge between systemic metabolic dysfunction and atrial cardiomyopathy through paracrine, inflammatory, fibrotic, and infiltrative pathways. This framework has direct therapeutic implications. Structured weight loss, cardiorespiratory fitness, alcohol reduction, and comprehensive risk-factor management can reduce AF burden and improve rhythm-control outcomes, although the magnitude of benefit varies across populations and trial designs. Incretin-based therapies have introduced a potentially important pharmacologic route to substrate modification. Semaglutide and tirzepatide produce substantial weight loss and favorable cardiovascular and heart-failure effects, while emerging observational and prospective data suggest lower AF incidence and post-ablation recurrence. However, evidence for reduced post-ablation recurrence remains predominantly non-randomized and is susceptible to residual confounding, treatment-selection effects, and healthy-user bias. Causality, weight-independent antiarrhythmic effects, optimal timing relative to ablation, and durability after treatment withdrawal remain unresolved. Observational sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor data support further investigation of cardiometabolic approaches to rhythm control, although randomized evidence has not consistently demonstrated benefit. Our review integrates mechanistic, imaging, lifestyle, pharmacologic, and electrophysiological evidence and proposes a practical model in which catheter ablation and cardiometabolic substrate modification are complementary strategies.

papers.title: From Association to Action: Personalizing Lifestyle Interventions in Multiple Sclerosis-A Critical Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Lifestyle factors are increasingly incorporated into multiple sclerosis (MS) care, but association, modifiability and therapeutic justification are not equivalent. This critical narrative review examines when a lifestyle exposure should become a clinical target after MS diagnosis. Evidence across physical activity and exercise, smoking, obesity and cardiometabolic health, diet, sleep, psychological stress, vitamin D and sun exposure, cognitive reserve and engagement, and alcohol is interpreted through the sequence modifiable exposure → post-diagnostic prognostic relevance → deliberate intervention → verified target modification (target engagement) → demonstrated clinical benefit, while distinguishing general-health benefit, MS-relevant clinical benefit and evidence for MS disease-course modification. The strength and completeness of this evidence vary substantially across domains. Smoking cessation and physical activity provide particularly strong grounds for clinical action, whereas several other exposures show larger gaps between prognostic association and intervention evidence. Multidomain intervention is not inherently personalized; personalization requires selection and prioritization of targets according to the intended outcome, strength of evidence, individual relevance and feasibility, followed by verification that the target changed and that the expected benefit occurred. Lifestyle intervention should complement, not substitute for, disease-modifying therapy, and no MS-directed intervention may be the appropriate personalized decision when a clinically relevant or sufficiently supported target is absent. The objective is therefore to support proportionate lifestyle decisions in which the intervention, intended outcome and therapeutic claim are matched to the available evidence and the individual clinical context.

papers.title: Evaluating the Efficacy of Comprehensive Nursing Care in Improving the Well-Being of Patients With Colon Cancer Who Developed Postoperative Sleep Disorders.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effect of comprehensive nursing care on the psychological state and related indicators of patients with postoperative sleep disorders after colon cancer surgery. We retrospectively selected 121 patients with sleep disorders who underwent colon cancer resection in our hospital between January 2021 and December 2023. After 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM), 52 patients were included in the routine nursing group and 52 in the comprehensive nursing group. Comprehensive nursing care, as documented in medical records, included psychological nursing, pain management, rehabilitation guidance and social support care. Data extracted from medical records and follow-up files showed that the comprehensive nursing group had greater reduction in Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS) and Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) scores after surgery than the routine nursing group (p < 0.05); the comprehensive nursing group also had shorter first anal exhaust time, first defecation time and hospitalization duration than the routine nursing group (p < 0.05). The complication incidence rate in the comprehensive nursing group was lower than the routine nursing group, but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.080). Improvements in all domains of the Short-Form 36 (SF-36) Health Survey in the comprehensive nursing group were greater than the routine nursing group (p < 0.05). The total score and several component scores of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index decreased more significantly in the comprehensive nursing group (p < 0.05). Comprehensive nursing care is a significant correlated between improved psychological state, rehabilitation-related indicators, quality of life and sleep quality in patients with postoperative sleep disorders after colon cancer surgery.

papers.title: Respiratory health risks associated with humidifier disinfectant exposure in South Korea: A systematic review and meta-analysis with exposure-response evaluation.
papers.abstract: Humidifier disinfectants (HDs) were used as household biocidal products to prevent microbial growth in humidifiers and were withdrawn from the South Korean market in 2011 following recognition of associated health risks. Although epidemiological studies have reported associations between HD exposure and various respiratory diseases, the overall strength of evidence and exposure-response relationships have not been comprehensively quantified. This study aimed to systematically review and quantitatively synthesize observational studies to evaluate the association between HD exposure and respiratory diseases and to assess exposure-response relationships across multiple exposure metrics. PubMed, Excerpta Medica Database, and the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature were searched through September 19, 2025. The primary outcome was the pooled odds ratio (OR) for respiratory disease risk among exposed versus non-exposed individuals. Secondary outcomes assessed exposure-response relationships using categorical and continuous exposure metrics. Seventeen observational studies conducted in South Korea were included. HD exposure was associated with a markedly increased risk of respiratory diseases (pooled OR 7.02, 95% CI 1.97-24.98), with the strongest association observed for lung injury (pooled OR 94.53, 95% CI 61.31-145.73). Age-stratified subgroup analyses exhibited significantly elevated risks across adult, pediatric, and mixed-age populations. Exposure-response analyses demonstrated significant associations across multiple categorical exposure metrics, including usage duration, daily usage hours, cumulative use hours, airborne concentration, cumulative exposure level, longer use during sleep, and HD use during sleep. Continuous exposure analyses indicated that affected individuals had significantly longer cumulative use hours than unaffected individuals (pooled standardized mean difference 0.197, 95% CI 0.069-0.325). This study provides quantitative evidence supporting strong associations between HD exposure and respiratory diseases and demonstrates consistent exposure-response relationships across multiple exposure metrics, supporting a causal relationship between inhalational exposure to HDs and adverse respiratory outcomes. This study provides comprehensive quantitative evidence that humidifier disinfectant exposure is strongly associated with respiratory diseases and demonstrates consistent exposure-response relationships across multiple exposure metrics. These findings strengthen causal inference for inhalational toxicity of humidifier disinfectants and highlight the importance of exposure assessment in environmental health risk evaluation. The results provide important evidence for environmental health policy, risk assessment, and prevention strategies for inhalation exposure to household biocidal products.

papers.title: Lifestyle Modifiers of Non-Infectious Uveitis: A Narrative Review of Current Evidence and Future Directions.
papers.abstract: Background: Non-infectious uveitis is a leading cause of preventable visual impairment and arises from complex interactions between genetic susceptibility, environmental exposures, and immune dysregulation. Purpose: To review current evidence regarding modifiable lifestyle factors that may influence the development, severity, recurrence, and outcomes of uveitis. This narrative review used structured searches of MEDLINE, PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews from database inception, last updated on 30 June 2026, supplemented by reference-list screening. Results: Diet, smoking, obesity, physical activity, sleep, psychological stress, alcohol consumption, and micronutrient status may affect uveitis through effects on systemic inflammation, Th1/Th17 immunity, regulatory T-cell function, oxidative stress, and the gut microbiome. Conclusions: Although the evidence remains limited and largely observational, lifestyle assessment may support personalized adjunctive care by considering the patient's uveitis phenotype, systemic comorbidities, treatment exposures and individual priorities. Lifestyle measures should support systemic health and shared decision-making without being presented as substitutes for established non-infectious uveitis treatment or as proven ocular disease-modifying interventions.

papers.title: Genetic Polymorphisms and Endocrine Pathways Associated with Problematic Digital-Media Use and Gaming Disorder: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Background: Problematic digital-media use and gaming disorder have emerged as important public health concerns, particularly among adolescents. Along with psychosocial factors, genetic susceptibility and neuroendocrine pathways may contribute to individual vulnerability to problematic digital-media use and gaming-related problems. Objectives: This review aims to summarize current evidence on the genetic polymorphisms and endocrine pathways associated with problematic digital-media use and gaming disorder, with emphasis on dopaminergic reward mechanisms and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis regulation. Methods: A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar for studies published up to 30 June 2026. Relevant human studies addressing genetic, epigenetic, endocrine, or related neurobiological mechanisms of problematic digital-media use and gaming-related behaviors were identified and narratively synthesized according to the principal biological pathways examined. Results: The available evidence suggests that genetic variants affecting dopaminergic neurotransmission (DRD2, COMT, DAT1, and DRD4), stress regulation (CRHR1, FKBP5), serotonergic signaling (SLC6A4), sleep-circadian regulation and other pathways (CHRNA4, NTRK3) may increase susceptibility to problematic Internet and gaming use. Excessive digital media exposure has been associated with alterations in dopaminergic signaling, stress and sleep-circadian regulation, including changes in hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity, cortisol secretion and melatonin secretion. These alterations may be related to differences in reward processing, sleep, and emotional regulation, as well as to compulsive digital behaviors. Bidirectional associations have also been reported between problematic digital-media use and depression, anxiety disorders, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Conclusions: Genetic and endocrine factors may contribute to a broader biopsychosocial vulnerability to problematic digital-media use and gaming-related problems. However, current evidence is insufficient to establish individual genetic variants or endocrine measures as clinically actionable biomarkers. Future research should prioritize large, adequately powered longitudinal studies with harmonized phenotypes, objective behavioral measures, genome-wide approaches, and independent replication to clarify the clinical relevance of biological markers and their potential role in risk prediction and personalized intervention.

papers.title: As Natural as Sleep: A Literature Study of Catholic Perspectives on Palliative Sedation.
papers.abstract: The Roman Catholic Church has a long-standing tradition of participating in the debates on the ethics of medical care. At the heart of the Church's reflections on this subject lies a deep respect for the dignity of individual patients and human life in general. This respect is also an expression of reverence for God and an acknowledgement of His sovereignty over human life. In the context of palliative care, these basic convictions have led to a strong rejection within Catholicism of those treatments that actively seek to end a patient's life (e.g. euthanasia, medical assistance in dying). Catholic views on palliative sedation, another possible end-of-life treatment, are less clear and forthright. As religion influences the attitudes of both patients and healthcare professionals towards end-of-life treatments, it is important to know and understand these views. This study aims to answer the following research question: what are the perspectives on palliative sedation within the catholic tradition? A comprehensive, systematic literature study was conducted, to identify and map the different perspectives on palliative sedation within the Catholic tradition. The methodology of a scoping review was adopted. The analysis of the sources was based on the Grounded Theory model and the model of systematic reviewing argument-based literature. This study draws on a wide range of sources, both academic and non-academic. The initial conclusion is that palliative sedation is welcomed as a means of alleviating patients' suffering. However, there are reservations. One such concern is that palliative sedation should be clearly distinguished from deliberate efforts to end the life of the patient. There are also concerns about the effect that the impaired consciousness could have on patients' spiritual lives.

papers.title: Psychological Burden and Mental Health Challenges Associated with Occupational Exposure to Zoonotic Pathogens: A Narrative Review and One Health Perspective.
papers.abstract: Zoonotic diseases continue to represent a major global public health challenge, requiring the coordinated efforts of professionals working at the human-animal-environment interface. Although occupational health strategies have traditionally focused on preventing biological hazards and infectious diseases, comparatively little attention has been given to the psychological burden associated with occupational exposure to zoonotic pathogens. Professionals such as veterinarians, animal shelter and rescue personnel, animal health workers, laboratory personnel, researchers, animal control staff, and wildlife conservation professionals are routinely exposed to biological, emotional and ethical challenges that may negatively affect mental health. Important sources of psychological burden include the perceived risk of infection, fear of transmitting pathogens to others, repeated exposure to animal suffering and euthanasia, prolonged outbreak-response activities, occupational uncertainty, and demanding working conditions. These occupational stressors have been associated with adverse mental health outcomes, including burnout, work-related stress, compassion fatigue, anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbances, potentially compromising individual wellbeing, workforce sustainability, and the effectiveness of zoonotic disease surveillance, research, and control. Despite increasing recognition of mental health as a fundamental component of occupational health, important knowledge gaps remain regarding the psychological consequences of occupational exposure to zoonotic pathogens. Greater integration of mental health into occupational health frameworks, together with strengthened research and evidence-based interventions tailored to these professional groups is essential to promote worker wellbeing and support resilient and sustainable systems.

papers.title: Clinical Evidence of Orally Administered Herbal Preparations for Supportive Cancer Care: A PRISMA Systematic Review of Randomized Clinical Trials (1990-2026).
papers.abstract: Orally administered herbal preparations have gained attention as complementary approaches in supportive cancer care; however, their clinical efficacy and safety remain uncertain. This systematic review critically evaluated evidence from randomized clinical trials investigating these interventions in patients with cancer. The review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines and was prospectively registered in PROSPERO. PubMed/MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, Springer Nature Link, CENTRAL, Scopus, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and WHO ICTRP were searched for English-language studies published from January 1990 through 8 September 2026. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2, and outcome-level certainty was evaluated using GRADE. Eight randomized clinical trials met the eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. The studies evaluated Gamiguibi-tang, Rikkunshito, holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum), Alcea digitata-Malva sylvestris, Annona muricata, Malva sylvestris-Althaea digitata, Jing Si herbal tea, and Renshen Yangrong Tang across heterogeneous cancer populations. Individual trials reported potentially favorable findings for sleep, fatigue, chemotherapy-induced anorexia, anxiety, salivary function, xerostomia, gastrointestinal symptoms, and quality of life. However, the Jing Si herbal tea trial found no statistically significant between-group differences in fatigue or quality of life, and exploratory ex vivo cytotoxicity findings did not demonstrate clinical antitumor efficacy. Meta-analysis was not feasible because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity. All evaluated outcomes were rated as very-low-certainty evidence, primarily because of risk of bias and serious imprecision. No serious intervention-related adverse events were identified in the published reports, but adverse-event monitoring was inconsistent and no trial was adequately powered to establish safety. The available evidence is insufficient to establish definitive efficacy or safety or to support routine clinical implementation. Adequately powered multicenter trials using botanically authenticated and chemically characterized preparations, clinically meaningful outcomes, interaction assessment, and long-term pharmacovigilance are required.
